title: Toronto 2026 Municipal Election Forecast
text:
All the data on this page come from synthetic voters. We use two large language models (LLMs) to act as Census-based Toronto residents and answer ballot questions. No real people were surveyed.
Toronto will elect a mayor and 25 ward councillors on Monday 26 October 2026. However, there are almost no public polling results for these races. Previous research has discussed the problem of forecasting with samples that do not represent actual voters (Wang et al. 2015). In this project, we aim to investigate:

Can a silicon sample — simulated voters generated by large language models and post-stratified to Census marginals — produce a transparent, reproducible forecast for all 26 Toronto municipal races, and what uncertainty and model disagreement does it imply?

Our prediction objective is to build a reproducible pipeline to estimate vote-share distributions and conditional win frequencies for each candidate in the mayoral race and all 25 ward councillor races, while also showing the uncertainty in the results.
We use silicon sampling (Argyle et al. 2023) in this project, while also considering the challenges and limitations of using LLMs to simulate voters (Bisbee et al. 2024; Heath and Alexander 2026).
Pipeline:
We use two large language model (LLM) providers to collect voting intentions from 3,042 synthetic personas, and we repeat the whole process three times. Since the synthetic sample may differ from Toronto’s population, we use post-stratification to calculate vote shares for each candidate. To include uncertainty, we use Method C, which combines Dirichlet sampling and multiplicative adjustment (SD = 4pp) to simulate possible results under various conditions. Finally, we report the prediction results from each provider and provide an equally weighted aggregate for comparison.
Headline Results:

Mayor: Olivia Chow received 97.7% of valid responses. However, after adding headlines, the prediction results became unstable, with Brad Bradford receiving 97–99% of valid responses on 20 October and Olivia Chow receiving 99% on 21 October. This means that the models were more affected by headlines than by the demographic profiles of the synthetic personas.
Wards: Based on the vote shares after post-stratification, the two providers disagreed on the leading candidate in 8 of 25 wards.
Uncertainty: When the assumed perturbation increased from 2pp to 6pp, the median leading candidate interval width rose from 33.6pp to 41.0pp.

title: Toronto 2026 Municipal Election Forecast
text:
Election Forecasts

The mayoral race






Figure 1: Mayoral vote shares by provider for the eight candidates with the largest pooled shares. Points are census post-stratified estimates of each candidate’s share of decided first preferences; bars are 95% simulation intervals. Both providers put almost all support on Olivia Chow.



In the figure, dots represent the estimates after post-stratification, and horizontal bars represent 95% simulation intervals. The two providers are shown in separate rows, and the figure shows the eight candidates with the highest pooled vote shares. Gemini gives Olivia Chow 99.9% of decided first-preference votes, while GPT-4o-mini gives her 94.7%. GPT-4o-mini also has a wider simulation interval, indicating more variation than Gemini. In our simulation, Chow’s win frequencies are 100% and 99.2% under Gemini and GPT-4o-mini, respectively. Although both providers give Chow very high win frequencies, these do not represent her actual probability of winning the election.






WarningMayoral mode collapse — read this before quoting any mayoral number



There is mode collapse in the production silicon sample. The prediction results fail to form a competitive distribution. The responses from both Gemini and GPT are mostly concentrated on the same candidate, Olivia Chow, who received 97.7% of all valid mayoral choices. To determine whether this was caused by ballot position, we conducted a diagnostic experiment and reproduced the pipeline under three ballot orders (see Diagnostics). Nevertheless, the same mode collapse appeared in the experiment. The issue has also been documented by Heath and Alexander (2026). In addition, the Daily Tracker indicates instability in the outputs. When the day’s headlines favour Brad Bradford, the same mode collapse shifts to him. Hence, no uncertainty method can create a competitive forecast from these results.

title: Toronto 2026 Municipal Election Forecast
text:
Provider Comparison






Figure 5: Simulation win frequency of each provider’s leading candidate, one row per ward. Red rows are the 8 wards where the providers name different leaders.



The map below shows the same disagreement geographically: every ward is labelled with its number and name, and each red ward also lists the two providers’ different leaders. Disagreement clusters in the old city core (Wards 04, 09, 13, 14), the Etobicoke lakeshore (03), and northern and southwestern Scarborough (20, 22, 23).






Figure 6: Wards where the two providers name different leaders (red, 8 wards) or the same leader (blue, 17 wards).




Reconciling two leader definitions
A leading candidate can be defined in two ways:

Provider point estimates: Average the results from three repeat cells.
Win frequencies: Average the results from 500 draws that resample cells and add uncertainty layers.

These two methods may identify different leading candidates in some wards.







Leader definition
Wards where providers disagree




Highest post-stratified point share (used on this site)
8: W03, W04, W09, W13, W14, W20, W22, W23


Highest simulation win frequency
7: W03, W04, W14, W15, W20, W22, W23



The website uses the point-share definition throughout (Figure 2, Figure 5, Figure 6, Table 2, and this section). The three definitional edge cases are instructive:

Ward 09: Based on vote-share point estimates, the two providers disagree. Gemini shows that three candidates’ vote shares are close (Marco Martins (30.1%), Alejandra Bravo (29.7%), and another candidate (29.3%)), with Marco Martins slightly leading, while GPT mainly supports Alejandra Bravo (82.5%). Conversely, based on win frequencies, both providers agree that Bravo is the leading candidate.
Ward 13: Based on vote-share point estimates, the two providers disagree. Gemini predicts that Chris Moise gets 57.0%, while GPT shows that Morgan Harris is leading with 24.7%, which is slightly higher than Chris Moise’s 24.0% under the same provider. Conversely, based on win frequencies, both providers agree that Moise is leading.
Ward 15: Based on vote-share point estimates, both providers agree that Rachel Chernos Lin is leading (48.0% from Gemini and 73.7% from GPT). Conversely, based on win frequencies, the two providers disagree. In Gemini’s simulation, Sheena Sharp has a higher win frequency (58.0%) than Rachel Chernos Lin (41.8%).

Two patterns matter regardless of definition:

The two providers disagree more than our uncertainty settings do. Among several wards with different prediction results, one provider gives its leading candidate a win frequency close to 90%, while the other gives its own leading candidate only about 35%. This indicates that the difference between providers is much larger than the change under any uncertainty setting we tested (see Forecast Uncertainty).
The two providers answer for different groups of personas. GPT-4o-mini answers “undecided” much more often than Gemini, especially in the mayoral election (19.4% vs. 0.8%; see Diagnostics). Since “undecided” answers are excluded from further predictions, each provider’s prediction is based on a different set of synthetic personas. We report predictions for the two providers separately, and the pooled column is only descriptive rather than a pooled forecast.

title: Toronto 2026 Municipal Election Forecast
text:
Forecast Uncertainty
Our forecast uncertainty comes from several sources. We used a Dirichlet model to simulate sampling uncertainty and added a 4-percentage-point standard deviation in Method C to approximate random changes in a real election. However, changes in turnout, unexpected campaign events, and systematic biases shared by the LLMs remain unaccounted for. Shirani-Mehr et al. (2018) show that bias and variance are two common sources of error in real election polls. Since the election has not yet taken place, we cannot measure these biases against actual results. Our uncertainty intervals may therefore be narrower than the true uncertainty in the election outcomes.
Below, we describe four sources of uncertainty and how we handle each one in our simulations.

LLM response variability: When collecting responses from synthetic voters, we asked each LLM three times and obtained different voting results because the temperature was set to 0.7. When performing the forecast simulations, we randomly select one of the three responses.
Dirichlet sampling uncertainty: shares ~ Dirichlet(\(n_{\text{eff}} \cdot \hat{s} + 0.5\)), where \(n_{\text{eff}} = (\sum_i w_i)^2 / \sum_i w_i^2\) is the Kish effective sample size of the post-stratified cell. This approximates how much the estimated vote shares could vary because they are based on a limited, unequally weighted synthetic sample.
Assumed forecast perturbation (Method C): We use a centred multiplicative perturbation \(s_k \propto s_k \cdot e^{\sigma \varepsilon_k}\), \(\varepsilon \sim N(0,1)\), with \(\sigma\) calibrated per race so that this layer alone gives the leader the target standard deviation (SD), with 4pp as the default. This keeps the candidates’ support rates summing to one, leaves candidates with 0% support unchanged, and approximately preserves the mean.
Real election uncertainty: We cannot model this uncertainty because we cannot account for turnout swings, campaign events, polling house effects, or systematic model errors.







Note“Win frequency” ≠ “probability of winning”



Throughout this site, simulation win frequency is the fraction of the 500 simulations in which a candidate has the highest support rate. It is not the candidate’s actual probability of winning the 2026 election: we have no ground truth against which to calibrate it, and LLMs have systematic biases that cannot be corrected. As discussed by Gelman et al. (2020) and Kay et al. (2016), it is important to communicate the gap between uncertainty in a simulation and uncertainty in the real world. A 100% win frequency in a graph does not mean that the election result is certain. Currently 15 of 52 race × provider units show a win frequency of exactly 100%, and 18 of 52 sit at or below 70%.



Sensitivity to the assumed perturbation scale






Figure 7: Sensitivity of the forecast to its one assumed parameter, the forecast-noise SD. (a) Each line joins one race-by-provider leader’s 95% interval width at SD 2, 4 and 6 percentage points; the dark line is the median. (b) Number of the 52 race-by-provider units whose leader wins every simulation draw; the dark bar is the published setting.



We wanted to know how changing the 4pp SD in Method C to 2pp or 6pp would affect the predictions. We therefore reran the forecast simulation three times, changing only the standard deviation. Panel (a) tracks each race × provider leader’s 95% interval width across the three simulations. The graph shows a linear upward trend as the standard deviation increases, confirming that more variation produces wider intervals. Panel (b) counts how many race × provider units still give their leader a 100% win frequency. As the standard deviation increases and more noise is included, the model becomes more uncertain, and the number of units with a 100% win frequency falls. Together they show that the width of our intervals and how many races look like a certain win are partly a modelling choice, not something the data pins down.
Beyond the perturbation scale, adding 0.5 to the Dirichlet parameters shrinks the overall support rates toward a uniform distribution, causing the leader’s support rate to decrease. The largest effect occurred in Ward 19, where the pseudocount accounts for 5.4% of the total Dirichlet parameters and the average leader support rate decreased by 4.7pp. Method C can also preserve the centre only approximately.

title: Toronto 2026 Municipal Election Forecast
text:
Silicon Sampling Diagnostics






Figure 8: Silicon-sample diagnostics. (a) Share of persona-race pairs that pick the same candidate under three different candidate orders. (b) Share of valid mayoral choices going to each of the eight most-chosen candidates. (c) Share of all production responses that were “undecided”.



In the previous section, we measured how uncertain the simulation results are. We now explore whether the synthetic voter responses generated by LLMs are reliable.
Candidate-order invariance. We first wanted to understand whether the sequence of candidates affected the LLMs’ decisions. In this diagnostic, we asked each persona about each race using three ballot orders: the original ballot order and two randomized orders. The mayoral choice was 100% order-invariant for both LLMs, confirming that the collapse was knowledge-driven rather than caused by ballot position. Ward-race choices, however, were invariant across all three ballot orders in only 56–63% of persona-race combinations, meaning that 37–44% changed their selection when the order changed. For example, in Ward 10, the same persona changed its vote when the ballot order changed. This shows that ward-level LLM responses are unstable and meaningfully order-sensitive, as Murray and Alexander (2026) also documented. We decided to retain the original ballot order rather than randomizing it.
Mayoral response concentration. In the results from the first day (2026-10-17), 99.9% of Gemini’s responses and 95.0% of GPT’s responses selected Chow; the remaining mass was spread across other minor candidates.
Provider undecided rates. We allow synthetic voters to select no candidate and instead respond “undecided”. In the mayoral race, GPT-4o-mini answered “undecided” 19.4% of the time, while Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite did so 0.8% of the time. In the ward races, GPT-4o-mini answered “undecided” 3.9% of the time, compared with 1.0% for Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite. We excluded undecided responses from estimation and counted only responses that selected a candidate.
To summarise, LLMs are sensitive to candidate order, may not represent the preferences of all voters, and have different response rates.
The full diagnostic design and report are available in docs/llm_diagnostic_experiment.md and docs/llm_diagnostic_report.md.

title: Toronto 2026 Municipal Election Forecast
text:
Data and Methods

Data sources
We use official City of Toronto data to construct our synthetic voter population, identify candidates in the 2026 municipal election, and provide historical and geographic context. The main datasets and their uses are summarized below.








Dataset
Use
Source




Ward Profiles, 25-ward model (2021 Census) (City of Toronto 2023)
Population frame and post-stratification marginals (ward × age × education)
Toronto Open Data


Official 2026 candidate lists (mayor, councillors, withdrawn) (City of Toronto 2026a)
Candidate roster and ballot names for all 26 races
toronto.ca elections


Official 2022 election results (City of Toronto 2022a)
Historical sanity checks; candidate/incumbency context
Toronto Open Data


2023 mayoral and Ward 20, 2024 Ward 15, 2025 Ward 25 by-election results
Updated historical context
Toronto Open Data


2022 Elections Voter Statistics (City of Toronto 2022b)
Ward-level turnout context
Toronto Open Data


Wards and Elected Councillors boundaries (City of Toronto 2026b)
Map geometry and ward validation
Toronto Open Data


Elected officials 2022–2026
Incumbent identification (name match)
Toronto Open Data



All datasets were downloaded using download_data.R. Their original URLs, file sizes, and SHA-256 checksums are recorded in sources.json to support reproducibility.
We use the 2021 Census Ward Profiles to build the population frame for post-stratification. Each ward is divided into four age groups and three education groups, giving us 12 demographic groups per ward and 300 across Toronto’s 25 wards. We restrict the population to residents aged 20 and older.
One limitation is that the available Census tables report age and education separately, rather than their joint distribution within each ward. We therefore estimate the proportion of each age–education group by multiplying the two marginal proportions: \(P(\text{Age}, \text{Education} \mid \text{Ward}) \approx P(\text{Age} \mid \text{Ward})\,P(\text{Education} \mid \text{Ward})\)
This assumes that age and education are independent within each ward, which may not hold in practice. As a result, the population weights used in post-stratification are approximations rather than exact Census counts for each demographic group.


Silicon sampling
Using 2021 Census data, we split Toronto’s population into 25 wards × 4 age groups × 3 education groups = 300 cells. We then generated 3,042 synthetic voters across the 300 cells based on each cell’s population aged 20 and older. We defined at least five personas per cell, so the final synthetic sample population may not reflect the true census population. Therefore, we assigned each persona a weight so that the sample represents the population during post-stratification.
In the experiment, we used two LLMs through OpenRouter: Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite and GPT-4o-mini. Each model was asked about every persona three times independently, using a temperature of 0.7. With 3,042 personas, two races per persona (mayoral and ward), two models, and three repetitions, this produced 36,504 requests.
In each prompt, we included the persona’s ward, age group, education level, and the candidates running in that race. The models were not given other personas’ responses, Census weights, candidate biographies, policy positions, or historical election results. We also randomized candidate order to reduce reliance on any single ballot ordering, although our previous results showed that ward-level responses remain sensitive to candidate order.
Responses were collected on October 18, 2026, and validated against a structured JSON format. Invalid responses were retried, and successful responses were cached to avoid unnecessary API calls. The final dataset contains 36,504 responses and is saved in processed/production/llm_responses.parquet.


What the model sees
Each request has a fixed system message (prompt version v1, llm/prompts.py) and a short user message. The system message tells the model it is simulating one Toronto resident in a municipal election survey, asks for a JSON reply of the form {"response_status": "valid_choice" | "undecided" | "not_voting", "candidate_id": ...}, and instructs it to base its choice only on the candidate names and the respondent’s demographics. The user message for persona P000446 and the Ward 4 race reads as follows (shown in ballot order; production shuffles the list per request):
Respond as the following Toronto resident:
- Ward: 4
- Age group: 30-44
- Education group: High school or less

Race: City Councillor for Ward 4 (you are a resident of Ward 4).

Candidates in this race (candidate_id: name):
- W04-C01: Corcoran, Michael
- W04-C02: Guerrera, Nadia
- W04-C03: King, Debbie
- W04-C04: McNally, Diana Chan
- W04-C05: Ogundipe, Bridget
- W04-C06: Pham, Adam
- W04-C07: Potega, Andy
- W04-C08: Raponi, Vanessa
- W04-C09: Weber, Holly
- W04-C10: Yuen, Steve

Return only the JSON object.
The daily tracker (prompt v2) adds the date, the election date, and up to 12 of that day’s Toronto headlines to the system message.


Post-stratification
Inspired by Wang et al. (2015) and Little (1993), we used post-stratification to adjust the synthetic responses to the real population by weighting each persona according to the population share of its ward and demographic cell. For each race, LLM provider, and repeat, we estimate each candidate’s vote share as a weighted proportion of the decided responses. \[\hat{s}_k \;=\; \frac{\sum_i w_i \,\mathbf{1}[\text{choice}_i = k]}{\sum_i w_i}\]
Undecided and not-voting replies are excluded from both the numerator and denominator because we want the candidate share among decided synthetic responses only. This is neither turnout nor the voting rate for the entire population.
For ward races, we sum over that ward’s personas only, while the mayoral race sums over all personas with citywide weights.
Since we repeated each query three times per persona, we take the average across repetitions as the point estimate. A descriptive pooled estimate averages the responses across all repetitions and LLM providers. We use it as a simple summary for readers, but never as “the” forecast.


Software
The language models are GPT-4o mini (OpenAI 2024) and Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite (Google DeepMind 2025), both reached through OpenRouter (OpenRouter 2026). The query pipeline is written in Python (Python Software Foundation 2025) with requests (Reitz 2025) and PyArrow (Apache Arrow Developers 2026), and tested with pytest (Krekel et al. 2026). Cleaning, post-stratification, simulation, and figures use R (R Core Team 2024) with dplyr (Wickham et al. 2023), tidyr (Wickham, Vaughan, et al. 2024), readr (Wickham, Hester, et al. 2024), readxl (Wickham and Bryan 2023), jsonlite (Ooms 2014), digest (Eddelbuettel 2024), nanoparquet (Csárdi and Mühleisen 2025), sf (Pebesma and Bivand 2023), ggplot2 (Wickham 2016), scales (Wickham et al. 2025), patchwork (Pedersen 2024), ggrepel (Slowikowski 2026), ragg (Pedersen and Shemanarev 2026), and systemfonts (Pedersen et al. 2024); tests use testthat (Wickham 2011) and code is formatted with styler (Müller et al. 2025). The site is built with Quarto (Allaire et al. 2026) and set in IBM Plex Sans (Abbink and Bold Monday 2018).

title: Toronto 2026 Municipal Election Forecast
text:
Discussion

What a silicon sample measures in a local election
Argyle et al. (2023) showed that LLMs conditioned on detailed personal backgrounds, such as demographic and partisan characteristics, could reproduce vote-choice patterns similar to those of real groups, a property they called algorithmic fidelity. However, our simulation lacks information such as party labels because Toronto’s municipal elections have no party labels. Thus, our personas contained only a ward, age band, and education band. The models had difficulty distinguishing voters based solely on those demographic features and relied more on their existing knowledge of the candidates. In our frozen run, Olivia Chow received 97.7% of valid votes, and Brad Bradford was not selected once, suggesting that the LLMs tended to vote for the candidates most familiar to them.


The collapse follows salience, not demographics
We observed almost all synthetic voters selecting the same candidate at the same time, an example of the mode collapse described by Heath and Alexander (2026). Initially, almost all synthetic voters selected Olivia Chow, but this trend began to change around 20 October according to our daily tracker. This observation suggests that the LLMs may not learn from the synthetic personas’ backgrounds and may instead reflect the news supplied to the models. After only the news headlines changed, both models gave Bradford 97–99% of decided votes on 20 October, when headlines reported that he was pulling ahead. On 21 October, when headlines criticized Bradford’s water plan, both models gave Chow about 99% of decided votes.
Bisbee et al. (2024) found that synthetic answers have far less variance than real ones and can shift with wording of the prompts as well as the date of the query. This is also supported by Santurkar et al. (2023), who found that simulating group opinions with LLMs could not recover the true differences between population groups. Wang et al. (2024) also showed that LLMs can suppress differences of opinion within a group.


Analyst choices are first-order
According to Murray and Alexander (2026), minor changes in some parameters can change silicon samples significantly. We saw the same pattern at every stage we varied. Changing the candidate order changed 37–44% of ward-race voting responses, and changing the provider changed the leading candidate in 8 of 25 wards. Changing the forecast-noise standard deviation from 2pp to 6pp increased the median 95% interval width by 7pp. Adding a day’s news headlines also changed the responses, as described in the previous section. Each effect is too large to attribute solely to sampling uncertainty, which is why we publish the two LLMs’ results separately and show each sensitivity rather than one blended number.


What post-stratification can and cannot fix
Wang et al. (2015) forecast a US election accurately from a heavily skewed sample of Xbox users, using multilevel regression and post-stratification to reweight a sample that is unrepresentative but still contains real differences between groups. Post-stratification cannot create differences that are not there, so even though we have 3,042 personas, if everyone gave almost the same answer, adding more personas does not mean adding more unique preference information. Thus, our current silicon-sample results are more suitable for measuring how the two LLMs perform differently than for use as a voter poll.

title: Toronto 2026 Municipal Election Forecast
text:
Limitations

No external calibration. Since no polling has been published for Toronto’s 2026 election and we did not calibrate against historical election errors, our simulation win frequencies should and must not be quoted as real winning probabilities (Gelman et al. 2020).
Mayoral mode collapse. In our mayoral race, 97.7% of valid synthetic votes concentrated on a single candidate, regardless of ballot order.
No turnout model. Only 2 of 36,504 replies were “not voting”, which does not reflect real-world voter participation. For example, even if a ward has a large young population, only a small proportion of that group may actually vote. Ignoring turnout and using only Census population weights rather than likely-voter weights will therefore bias the results.
Informative undecided responses. GPT-4o-mini returned “undecided” for 19.4% of mayoral queries, and we excluded all those responses during post-stratification. If young people are more likely than older people to respond “undecided”, excluding those answers will reduce the influence of the young population and make our synthetic results less representative (Bisbee et al. 2024).
Census independence approximation. We assumed that age and education are independent within each ward, although they could be correlated in reality.
Provider disagreement dominates method choices. We used two LLMs to predict the same 25 ward councillor elections, and they chose different leading candidates in 8 of them. A simple average of the vote shares from the two LLMs would hide this difference. We therefore include each model’s selection in our report.
Small effective samples. Although we have 3,042 personas in total, each ward contains only a small portion of them. The Kish effective sample size \(n_{\text{eff}}\) in ward elections is only about 79–165, leading to sparser Dirichlet samples and wider uncertainty intervals. Adding 0.5 as a Dirichlet pseudocount can also shrink the leading candidate’s support toward a uniform prior. In the ward with the largest effect, this shrinkage is approximately 4.7pp. When applying Method C, we want the predicted centre to remain the same while adding uncertainty. However, normalization after the multiplicative perturbation may cause the mean response to shift.
Simulated voters are not voters. The entire electorate is synthetic; the forecast measures what two LLMs say about a Census-shaped persona frame (Bisbee et al. 2024).

title: Toronto 2026 Municipal Election Forecast
text:
Conclusion and Future Work
To summarise, we’ve run silicon sampling with census post-stratification and produced a complete, reproducible forecast for the upcoming Toronto mayoral and city councillor election.
Our results show that without news, the models collapsed onto a single candidate: in our initial frozen experiment, 97.7% of valid synthetic votes selected Chow, regardless of ballot order. With a day’s news headlines, the entire synthetic preference moves to whichever candidate the headlines favour. Ward races are more varied, and the two providers disagree about the leading candidates in 8 of 25 wards. Our uncertainty has not yet been calibrated to errors in real elections, but we used repeated LLM responses, Dirichlet sampling, an extra perturbation in Method C, and sensitivity analysis across target standard deviations to understand the possible uncertainties.
Natural next steps, in order of value:

Calibrate after 26 October. Score every provider forecast against the official results with Brier and log scores, and measure the real coverage of the simulation intervals — turning the current honest disclaimer into an empirical error estimate.
Model the undecided. Treat “undecided” as an outcome to be modelled (e.g., a separate post-stratified rate with principled allocation) instead of dropping it.
Correct mode collapse following Heath and Alexander (2026) (semantic similarity rating) and re-test whether the mayoral race becomes informative.
Strengthen the frame by obtaining age × education joint counts (e.g., PUMF) to remove the independence approximation, and adding a turnout layer informed by City of Toronto (2022b).
Combine providers with an explicit hierarchical model that treats provider as a random effect, instead of reporting arms separately.

Complete workflow

Rscript download_data.R && Rscript prepare_data.R

# 2. Population frame and synthetic personas (seeded)

  --seed 20261026 --budget-usd 3.75

# 4. Post-stratification and Method C forecast draws (md5-guarded)
Rscript R/10_llm_poststratify.R processed/production/llm_responses.parquet centered

# 5. Tests (164 R expectations, 117 Python tests; no network)
Rscript tests/run_tests.R
python3 -m pytest tests/python -q

Validation
The committed forecast passed 22/22 automated checks (md5 preservation, 26 races / 243 candidates / 300 census cells, draw-simplex sums to 1 within \(1.4\times10^{-15}\), win frequencies sum to 1 per race × provider, no NA/NaN, seed replay identity) — see processed/forecast/validation_report.md. AI-use declaration
We used the AI tools listed below for coding assistance, analysis, and editorial review. We reviewed and verified any AI-generated material before incorporating it into the project.

OpenCode with MiMo-V2.6-Flash (Xiaomi, free tier; model identifier mimo-v2.6-flash), 17–19 October 2026. Jingwen Zhong used it as a coding agent to write and test the OpenRouter query pipeline (llm/), the simulated-data pipeline and its tests (R/07–R/10, R/simulation_helpers.R, tests/testthat/test-07 to test-11, tests/python/), the ballot-order diagnostic (scripts/analyze_llm_diagnostic.py, docs/), the uncertainty comparison (experiments/), and the first version of the website and website/make_figures.R.
Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic; model identifier claude-opus-5-5), 19 and 22 October 2026. Jingwen Zhong used it as a coding agent to fix and redesign the website figures and tables (website/make_figures.R, website/make_daily.R), build the shared design system (website/theme_site.R, website/custom.scss), add the software citations, remove setwd() from scripts and tests, run styler, add the submission-deadline guard to the GitHub Action, and review the project against the rubric. It also drafted website prose: the Discussion section, figure and table captions, the “What the model sees” and Software subsections, and edits to the Overview and Daily Tracker text. We checked every number in that prose against our data and edited it.
Cursor as a coding agent, 20–22 October 2026. Siyi Zhu used it for the daily tracker and its GitHub Action. On 20 October the model was Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic; model identifier claude-opus-5-5). It wrote .github/workflows/daily-forecast.yml and scripts/run_daily.sh, added the Daily Tracker to the website, and set the workflow to stop after 25 October 2026. On 21 October the model was Grok 4.7 (xAI; model identifier grok-4.7). It moved the Daily Tracker onto the single page (website/index.qmd, removing website/daily.qmd) and added backup schedule times after a scheduled run did not start. On 22 October the model was again Grok 4.7 (grok-4.7). It compared the repo to the assignment rubric, moved downloaded files from raw/ to data/01-raw_data/, updated the scripts that read them, and removed the phrase “kind of” from the discussion. Siyi checked the diffs and ran the git commit and push. These Cursor sessions are separate from the Claude Code session listed above.
ChatGPT (OpenAI; GPT-6), 25 October 2026. Jingwen Zhong used ChatGPT to review the published website and README against the assignment rubric, identify grammatical errors, suggest more concise wording, and check whether the documentation accurately describes the implemented workflow. The authors reviewed suggested changes before incorporating them. ChatGPT was not used to generate the synthetic voting responses.

The two language models that generate the synthetic responses, openai/gpt-4o-mini and google/gemini-2.5-flash-lite via OpenRouter, are the object of study rather than writing aids; every response they returned is kept in the repository.
